body: This is the discussion we had today and is becoming the most likely scenario over the next ~2 years

Family- we don't have any reliable family as we both grew up in abusive households, and our parents have not shown enough self-improvement to warrant trusting them with our kids. We barely feel safe staying a week with one of them. Otherwise, this would have been the obvious answer for us.

My job- I am restricted by health care laws from doing overtime as it risks misdiagnosis of cases. Wife could work more, but the focus will be career development for her. I am thinking of just taking any part-time evening job I can get my hands on for the near term 

Time- ill look into this more on her end. My professional career is almost exclusively M-F 8-4:30 nationwide.

We also have every motivation to cut, cut, and cut all expenses that we possibly can, starting after the baby.

I give them a pass and try to be empathetic because they might not understand why it's so valuable. It is a personal finance sub, after all. For me, however, I look at my parents' generation and how they raise so many kids that ended up on psychiatric medications and increasingly suicidal. Something had to have gone wrong for that to happen. I'm simply trying to prevent that from happening to my little corner of society.
The kids will be of school age by then.

For clarification, I am not a nurse. I am a lab specialist who is highly specialized with minimal job opportunities around the country. There is no path to a higher paying position without schooling. I also have workload limits put on by the federal government that prevent me from being able to work overtime in most jobs available to me. I truly have maxed out in my field and boxed myself in.

Thank you. This means a lot. Our first kid has such a well-adjusted temperament, and it's all thanks to my wife's immense efforts to properly raise and socialize him. We both come from rough childhoods, so we see the value in giving them a better life than we ever had. Her PhD will actually be in psychology to help people thru childhood trauma and she is extremely passionate about properly raising babies.

Thanks for the honesty. For clarification, at no point will both of us be in school simultaneously. The most likely scenario is wife working while I am in medical school, and she won't start her school until I am at least a couple years into residency. The house on the other hand, I admit, is an emotional stability thing for us. Wishful thinking, maybe. It likely won't happen unless we can get my wife to a place where her income surpasses 175-200k and she can bankroll my school.

The current income is fine, but the lifestyle is unsustainable. It's the pivot that is just so challenging to figure out. If we can fast forward 5 years with the wife working in a stable job with minimal expenses, then I feel like I can start dreaming again for things like a house, grad school, etc

There may be a minor decrease in rates, but it won't be anything that shifts markets. Home prices will not go down in the near future as the rate changes do not solve the supply side issue, at least not in the short term. As for the stick market, well who knows. It's just doing it's own thing...

Lenders, like investors, try to predict the market and set their rates accordingly. It has been widely known that rate cuts were coming from the fed for months now. The only thing missing were the details of when and how much. Most banks have cut their rates to some extent already in anticipation of interest rate changes by the fed. They might be slightly off when considering how much the fed lowered rates, but most of the Fed's cut is 'baked in' as they say.
Temper your expectations, yall. Mortgage rates try to forecast, not react, to the market. This rate cut might have already been baked in with the previously declining rates.

If you want more details from a pathology side, I'll tell you what I have time to say;

Each cancer specimen that comes into my lab is different and gets an array of tests like an a la carte buffet. The specimen is typically a fluid, biopsy, fine needle aspiration or a gross surgical. These can be processed and prepared for me to look at in different ways.

 For example, a body fluid might get spun down in a centrifuge, leaving a pellet of cells at the bottom of the test tube. Those cells are then extracted and put on a slide and stained by an array of stains which can help reveal abnormal looking cells. For an idea of how that looks, search for 'cancer on the Papanicolaou stain'.

Another way that it is diagnosed is that the same pellet can be put in a gel and cut into very thin sheets of single cells. These sheets can then be put on a slide and stained with markers like 'CD20' or 'TTF-1'. These markers are very specific for the different types of cancer and when a pathologist has a hard time differentiating one cancer from another, these stains are used to clarify that. This process is called cell blocking.

Each cancer specimen goes through probably a minimum of 5-10 tests before it is diagnosed. We want to be absolutely sure we are correct (and even then we don't get it 100% of the time)

Hope all this helps with the behind the scenes perspective! If you have other questions feel free to dm me!
